title: The earth-formed animals as nations in the Church, and ruling as the image
english: In the same way, by saying that all the birds and all the wild animals were now formed by God, Scripture gives us no room at all to say that they came into being earlier and only a part of them now. For this reason God gives no command among these about eating seeds. The creatures that enter paradise do not eat grass, but every tree beautiful to the sight and good for food—and above all, from the tree of life, Christ who gives life. And it is possible to say that these living creatures are the nations—these wild animals gathered by God in the Church—or that paradise today is a place of horses, herds of swine, camels, and flocks of sheep. No, philosopher, it is not so. No, philosopher, it is not so. Rather, God’s saying “Let them rule all the earth” and “let them have dominion over it and over everything in it” (Genesis 1:28)—this is the chief point of making the human being in God’s image and of his ruling all the earth.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG 18 In Genesim de creatione u01-rem-early
orientation: Eustathius is still distinguishing the Genesis 2 animals formed from the earth from the earlier water-born creatures, and now turns to what it means for humanity to rule.

title: The second ruler and the plural 'let us make'
english: Since God rules all the earth and everything in it, and in the same way appointed the human being as a second ruler over all the earth and everything in it, I say that this is what it means for the human being to be made in God's image and in God's likeness. And God said, “Let us make a human being in our image and in our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). But to whom did he say it? Let us investigate, philosopher.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG 18 In Genesim de creatione u01-rem-mid
orientation: Eustathius is answering the philosopher, having just identified humanity's ruling over the earth as the chief point of being made in God's image; he now states this as his own conclusion and turns to the plural 'let us make' in Genesis 1:26.

title: The plural 'let us make' reveals a co-creator
english: For by saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being in our image and in our likeness’” (Genesis 1:26), the text throws in a question for us to understand: to whom was he saying “let us make”? After saying, “And God said, ‘Let us make a human being,’” it goes on to say, “And God made the human being; in God's image he made him; male and female he made them” (Genesis 1:27). So the meaning of “let us make” indicates that there is a co-creator, and it introduces one of equal address. For just as the Father who said “let us make a human being” is God, so also the one to whom he said “let us make” is God, since the deity of both persons is one—both the one who said, “Let us make a human being in God's image and in God's likeness,” and the one who made the human being. The voice “let us make” presents the all-holy and unvarying deity of the Father and the Son. For the image of God is simple and uncompounded, being fire in nature.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG 18 In Genesim de creatione u01-rem-close
orientation: Eustathius is answering the philosopher's question about whom God addressed in Genesis 1:26, arguing that the plural verb introduces a co-creating person.
